classification.difficultyReason: Derive centre distances from tangent-circle radii, then prove the triangle is right-angled.

content.prompt:
The diagram shows three circles with centres A, B and C. The circles touch without overlapping.

Show that triangle ABC is right-angled.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 7, three tangent circles below the stem
spec.description: Unfilled externally tangent circles, with A above, C lower left and B lower right; centre points joined as triangle ABC and external diameter labels retained.
spec.mathematics: Radii A = 6 cm, B = 4 cm and C = 2 cm. Centre distances AB = 10 cm, AC = 8 cm and BC = 6 cm. Coordinates place AC and BC perpendicular without adding a right-angle marker to the question.
spec.answerVisibility: Diameter givens and centre labels are visible; derived distances and the right-angle conclusion are absent.

answer.short: $AC^2+BC^2=8^2+6^2=100=AB^2$. By the converse of Pythagoras’ theorem, $\angle ACB=90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
The radii are $6\text{ cm}$, $4\text{ cm}$ and $2\text{ cm}$. Since the circles touch externally, each centre distance is the sum of the two radii.

$$\begin{align*}AB&=6+4=10\text{ cm}\\BC&=4+2=6\text{ cm}\\AC&=6+2=8\text{ cm}\\AC^2+BC^2&=8^2+6^2\\AC^2+BC^2&=100\\AB^2&=10^2=100\end{align*}$$

Thus $AC^2+BC^2=AB^2$. By the converse of Pythagoras’ theorem, triangle ABC is right-angled at C.
